related_questions.question: Are at-home COVID tests still accurate?

text_blocks.snippet: Yes, at-home COVID tests, specifically antigen tests, are generally still accurate and should detect newer variants of the virus. While they may be less sensitive than PCR tests, they have a low false-positive rate and offer quick results, making them a useful tool. However, it's recommended to repeat testing after a negative result, especially if you have symptoms, to minimize the risk of a false negative.
snippet_highlighted_words: Yes, at-home COVID tests, specifically antigen tests, are generally still accurate

list.title: Accuracy:
list.snippet: At-home COVID tests, which are typically antigen tests, are designed to detect the presence of specific proteins (antigens) from the SARS-CoV-2 virus. These tests are generally reliable, but they may not be as sensitive as PCR tests, meaning they might not always detect the virus in very early stages of infection or in people with low viral loads.

list.title: Newer Variants:
list.snippet: Studies and expert opinions indicate that at-home antigen tests are still effective against newer COVID-19 variants. The antigen targeted by these tests has remained relatively stable even as the virus evolves.

list.title: False Negatives:
list.snippet: A key point to remember is that at-home antigen tests can produce false negative results, particularly in the early stages of infection or if the viral load is low. This is why the FDA recommends repeating tests after a negative result, especially if symptoms are present.

list.title: False Positives:
list.snippet: At-home tests have a low false-positive rate, meaning it's unlikely they will incorrectly indicate a positive result.

list.title: Symptomatic Testing:
list.snippet: If you have symptoms of COVID-19, it's crucial to test, even with a negative result. Repeat testing after a negative result can help reduce the chance of a false negative.

list.title: Reporting Results:
list.snippet: The FDA encourages voluntary reporting of both positive and negative test results to help track the spread of the virus.

text_blocks.snippet: The most accurate COVID-19 test is the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test. It is a laboratory-based test that detects the virus's genetic material (RNA) in a sample collected from the nose or throat. PCR tests have a sensitivity of over 99%, meaning they correctly identify almost all infected individuals.

Other COVID-19 tests, such as rapid antigen tests, are less accurate but provide faster results. They are typically used for screening purposes and may not detect all infected individuals, especially if viral loads are low.
